prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and thereby revealing new channels through which trade affects productivity and welfare

statement.case_for: I ranked B039 first in my opening view and B010 third. After reading colleagues' arguments I now prefer B010 as the single-achievement proposal. The Melitz (2003) model moved trade analysis from industries to firms. It explains why only some firms export, why exporters are systematically different, and how reallocation across firms produces gains from trade beyond comparative advantage. It has also been tested against firm-level register and customs data in many countries, so its predictions are visibly checked against data. That is the kind of theory-plus-credible-evidence combination I weigh most heavily. Attribution is workable with two names. Melitz is the central model, and Helpman's broader record (monopolistic competition in trade, and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus FDI) supports co-recognition. The paradigm is more than twenty years old and is standard in teaching, empirical work and trade-policy evaluation. Several colleagues from different fields independently ranked it in their top three. I do not treat that as scientific merit, but it suggests the case does not depend on one subfield's taste.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are important empirical and theoretical precursors who are not credited on this ballot, and Redding is omitted from a two-name award. Some of the policy-relevant quantitative results, such as the size of the selection gains, depend on parametric assumptions like Pareto productivity draws. Trade was also recognised in 2008, so the Committee must be satisfied that this is a distinct advance and not a continuation of new trade theory. In addition, B039 may be the more transformative case in scientific terms, since it built a whole field, and I may be underweighting it because its core cross-country identification is contested.

responses.point: Krusell ranked B039 sixth. He values the field-building contribution of Persson, Tabellini and Besley, but flags its proximity to the 2024 institutions-and-prosperity prize and notes that Persson is a past committee member.
responses.response: The 2024 proximity is a fair point and I gave it too little weight in my opening ranking. Electoral rules, constitutions and fiscal policy are substantively distinct from colonial-origins institutions and growth, but the Committee would still have to justify the marginal novelty. The Persson connection is a disclosed matter and not something I treat as disqualifying, though it adds process complexity. Together with my own concern that cross-country constitutional identification is contested, this has led me to move B010 ahead of B039. I keep B039 as my first alternative because I still think the field-building case is strong.

responses.point: Hassler ranked B010 first. He argues that heterogeneous-firm trade models go well beyond the 2008 new-trade-theory prize, with Melitz as the central model, Helpman as a major parallel contribution and Redding as more of a successor. He also notes that credit is somewhat fragmented because Eaton-Kortum and Bernard-Jensen sit outside the ballot.
responses.response: I agree on distinctness from 2008. The firm-level micro-data agenda is what separates this from the Krugman-era contribution. I also agree that two names are cleaner than three. I would qualify his confidence on one point. The fragmentation he mentions is real, and the Committee should word the citation around firm heterogeneity and selection, without implying it covers the whole of quantitative trade. That framing leaves room for the precursors without crediting them wrongly. I would not treat the omission of Eaton-Kortum or Bernard-Jensen as fatal, but I would not call attribution fully resolved.

responses.point: Teorell ranked B019 first and B039 third. He regards Persson, Tabellini and Besley as a clear core trio with distinct credit and a field-defining influence that reaches political science, and he discloses a co-authorship with Persson.
responses.response: I agree the attribution in B039 is cleaner than in most macro candidates, which is why I ranked it first. The disclosed co-authorship with Persson means his ranking should be read with that in mind. The remaining weakness is how well constitutional and electoral-rule effects are identified. Natural experiments are harder to interpret than they look, and these cross-country results are still contested. That gap between conceptual influence and settled evidence is why I now put B010 ahead, where selection and exporter premia are confirmed repeatedly in firm-level data.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would accept a two-name award that omits Redding and the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum precursor strand.
How robust the quantitative gains-from-trade magnitudes are to the distributional assumptions behind the selection mechanism.
Whether B010 is judged a distinct advance beyond the 2008 new-trade-theory prize.
Whether the 2024 institutions prize reduces the marginal case for B039 enough to make it a lesser alternative.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It documents no co-authorship or institutional tie with Helpman, Melitz or the credited names on B039 and B037. Its only documented overlap with the committee is an institutional one at Stockholm University (2010-17) with the IIES macro group (Hassler, Krusell). That is not a co-authorship, and those members are not candidates.
